title: The rabbi's son
hookLine: another tale: a son is kept from his true teacher by his father's doubts until too late
tomorrow: what if someone argued your case to heaven, every single time?

lines: A SON WHO FEELS SOMETHING MISSING.
cards: A tab stays open on the laptop for weeks: an application, a sign-up, a message never sent. Every week brings a fresh, sensible reason to wait.
Rebbe Nachman told a tale about exactly that, and it answers the question plainly. The rabbi's son never reached his teacher because every delay looked reasonable.
A rabbi's only son, a gifted student, feels something missing, and longs to travel to a certain tzaddik, a holy teacher. His father doubts the man. Still, they set out.

teach.b: On the first trip the horses stumble and the wagon tips. The father says: a sign from heaven. They turn back.
On the next try an axle breaks. Another sign.
On the third, at an inn, a merchant says he knows the tzaddik, and speaks of him with contempt. That settles it. They go home.
Here the tale turns dark, so gently: the son falls ill and dies. Later he comes to his father in a dream, burning with anger, and tells him to go. The father goes.

teach.h: THE MERCHANT WAS THE EVIL ONE.
teach.b: At the same inn he meets the same merchant, who now says who he is: the Evil One. He was behind every stumble.
The son and the tzaddik, he says, were a lesser light and a greater light, and if they had met, the Messiah would have come. Some readers hear in it how hard the world pushes back on the good things.

And it's honest about something ordinary: obstacles aren't always signs. Sometimes they're just obstacles, and the voice calling them signs is the doubt that was already there. The father wasn't wicked.
He was careful, a little proud, and slow. That's what makes the tale hurt. It never asks anyone to stop being careful.
It asks you to notice when careful has quietly turned into never.

how: Rebbe Nachman's tales are read aloud and studied in Breslov circles and beyond; 'The Rabbi and His Only Son' is often taught as a warning against letting doubts, dressed up as signs, keep a person from what calls them.

o: a story of a son who rebels and leaves his father's house
a tale of a son kept from his teacher by doubt and delay
a teaching on how a rabbi chooses the one who follows him

games.q: who's who in the tale — tap the pairs.
p: read each mishap as a sign
the son tells his father to go

s: in the tale, the father is a wicked man
he's careful, a little proud, and slow; that's what makes it hurt.
the merchant at the inn turns out to be the Evil One
he was behind every stumble on the road.
the tale teaches that every obstacle is a sign from heaven
the father read them as signs; the tale shows they were obstacles.

games.q: for months your friend has meant to visit her grandfather. first a test, then a cold, now rain. she asks if it's a sign she shouldn't go. what does the rabbi's son say?
o: obstacles aren't always signs. go this weekend, rain or not.
three in a row probably means wait for a clearer moment.
only go once it's easy, or the visit won't mean much.
games.why: the father read every mishap as heaven's no, and the meeting never happened. the tale's warning: don't wait too long.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you keep meaning to do that feels like a calling: a class, a call, a skill, a visit. Name the wish in a few words, then the obstacle that keeps winning, the one that always sounds reasonable.
Then shape one small plan for when it shows up again: when that reason comes, I'll take this one step anyway.

wordCard.voice: The rabbi's son: Rebbe Nachman's tale of a son kept from his teacher by his father's doubts, read as signs, until it was too late.

orig.note: Hebrew: a righteous one; in Hasidic life, a holy teacher and guide.

carryVoice: For today: don't wait too long, because an obstacle isn't always a sign from above. Until tomorrow.
